message:
Hi. I'm off to Lisbon next week for a three-day work trip, my first time in Portugal, and I want to travel carry-on only this time, after the airline lost my case in the spring.

Could you suggest three things to do in Lisbon on a free evening? And how do I say "thank you" in Portuguese? Is it different depending on who's saying it? And is tipping expected in restaurants there, or is that more of an American thing?

My wheeled bag measures 56 × 36 × 23 cm including the wheels and handle, and packed it weighs 9 kg. Will it meet the carry-on limit?

Also, recommend a packing approach: rolling or folding for work shirts? I need a short out-of-office message that's professional but not stiff, since most of my contacts are clients rather than colleagues. And what's a good colour for a luggage tag so it's easy to spot? I'm flying back on the Friday evening, straight after a full day of meetings, so anything that makes the return journey less stressful is welcome.

Thanks a lot.
response:
Here's everything, starting with the bag, since that's the one with the most at stake.

## Will your bag meet the carry-on limit?

**It depends on the airline, and you haven't said which one.** At 56 × 36 × 23 cm and 9 kg, your bag is right on the edge of several common limits. A few examples (check your airline's website, as policies change):

| Airline | Cabin bag limit | Your bag (56 × 36 × 23 cm, 9 kg) |
|---|---|---|
| **TAP Air Portugal** (economy) | 55 × 40 × 20 cm, 8 kg | ✗ 1 cm too long, 3 cm too deep, 1 kg over |
| **British Airways** | 56 × 45 × 25 cm, 23 kg | ✓ Fits |
| **easyJet** (large cabin bag, paid add-on) | 56 × 45 × 25 cm, 15 kg | ✓ Fits, if you've paid for the bigger bag |
| **Ryanair** (Priority) | 55 × 40 × 20 cm, 10 kg | ✗ 1 cm too long, 3 cm too deep |
| **Lufthansa** (economy) | 55 × 40 × 23 cm, 8 kg | ✗ 1 cm too long, 1 kg over |

Some things to check:

- **Depth is the most likely problem.** At 23 cm, your bag is 3 cm over the common 20 cm limit. Soft bags can sometimes be squeezed into the sizer at the gate, but hard-shell ones can't.
- **On budget airlines, the base fare often includes only a small under-seat bag.** A wheeled cabin bag usually requires a paid add-on.
- **Weight matters as well as size.** Some airlines, especially TAP and Lufthansa, have an 8 kg limit, and some weigh bags at the gate.

If your bag doesn't fit your airline's rules, move a kilo or two into a personal item such as a laptop bag. Gate staff are much stricter about a bag that obviously bulges than one that's slightly over the limit on paper.

## Three things to do on a free evening

1. **Watch the sunset from a miradouro (viewpoint).** Miradouro da Senhora do Monte and Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara have some of the best views over the city's rooftops and the river. Arrive about 30 minutes before sunset.
2. **Hear fado in Alfama.** Fado is Portugal's traditional, very emotional music. Many small restaurants in the Alfama and Mouraria districts host live performances over dinner. Book ahead if you can, and expect people to be quiet during the songs.
3. **Eat at the Time Out Market, then walk up to Bairro Alto.** The market (Mercado da Ribeira) has stalls from some of the city's best chefs. It's easy and quick if you're tired after work, and you can try lots of local dishes. Bairro Alto, a short walk away, gets lively later in the evening with small bars spilling onto the streets.

Wear comfortable shoes. Lisbon is very hilly, and its cobblestone pavements get slippery.

## How to say "thank you" in Portuguese

Yes, the word changes, but it depends on **who is speaking**, not who you're thanking:

- **Obrigado** (oh-bree-GAH-doo) if you're a man.
- **Obrigada** (oh-bree-GAH-dah) if you're a woman.

The word literally means "obliged." For "thank you very much," say **muito obrigado/obrigada** (MWEE-too). People will appreciate the effort.

## Tipping

**It isn't expected the way it is in the US.** Service staff in Portugal are paid a proper wage, and tipping is optional. Common practice:

- **Cafés and casual meals:** round up the bill or leave some coins.
- **Sit-down restaurants:** 5–10% if you were happy with the service. Nobody will mind if you leave nothing.
- **Check the bill first.** Some places, particularly in tourist areas, add a service charge.

One thing to know: restaurants often bring small dishes to the table at the start of a meal, such as bread, olives or cheese (*couvert*). They're not free. If you eat them, they'll be on the bill. If you don't want them, just say "não, obrigado/obrigada" and they'll take them away.

## Packing work shirts: fold them

**Fold** collared shirts rather than rolling them. Rolling is great for T-shirts, jumpers and casual clothes, but it creases the fronts of shirts and can crush collars. A few tips:

- **Button the top and middle buttons** before folding, and fold along the natural seams.
- **Put each shirt in a dry-cleaning bag or wrap it in tissue paper.** The slippery layer stops the fabric from creasing against itself.
- **Pack the shirts flat on top**, with rolled items filling the gaps around them.
- **Hang them in the bathroom when you arrive** and run a hot shower. The steam drops out most creases.

## Out-of-office message

> **Subject:** Out of office: [dates]
>
> Hi,
>
> Thanks for your email. I'm travelling for work from [date] to [date], with limited access to email, so my replies may be slower than usual.
>
> If your message is urgent, please contact [Name] at [email/phone], who'll be happy to help. Otherwise, I'll get back to you when I return on [date].
>
> Best wishes,
> [Your name]

## Luggage tag colour

Go for something bright that isn't black, navy or grey: **neon orange, lime green or hot pink** stand out best on airport belts and in overhead lockers.

Even with carry-on only, a tag is still worth having. Bags are sometimes taken at the gate and put in the hold when the flight's overhead bins are full, especially wheeled bags on full flights. Given your experience in the spring, consider a **Bluetooth tracker** (such as an AirTag) in the bag too.

## Making Friday's journey less stressful

- **Pack Friday morning before your meetings**, or better, Thursday night. Leave only your toiletries to add at the last minute.
- **Check out and leave your bag at the hotel reception** if you're going back there, or check whether you can bring it to the meeting venue so you can go straight to the airport.
- **Check in online** and download your boarding pass to your phone.
- **Allow plenty of time at Lisbon airport.** It's close to the city (about 20–30 minutes by taxi or Uber, or the metro's red line). But security queues there can be very long, especially on Friday evenings. Aim to arrive at least two hours before your flight.
- **Keep your liquids bag and laptop at the top of your bag** for a quick security check.
- **If you have spare time**, the airport is a good place for a last *pastel de nata* (custard tart).

Have a great trip!
